catalog_quote: Al nivel de la palabra, el acento es trocaico pero sensible al peso silábico, al igual que otras lenguas pano (véase Valenzuela 2003: 107 para shipibo-konibo, Zariquiey 2011: 124 para kashibo-kakataibo). Dicho de otro modo, el acento, generalmente, recae en la primera sílaba, ya sea liviana (2a) o pesada (2b). Sin embargo, cuando la segunda sílaba es pesada, el acento es atraído por esta (2c-2e). (2a) 'a.na „lengua‟ (2b) 'toh.pi „verruga‟ (2c) o.'moh „peca‟ (2d) is.'pan „patilla, sien‟ (2e) ten.'ton „manzana de adán‟ [p.23] ... El prefijo forma una sola unidad prosódica con la raíz a la que se adjunta, de modo que se halla un solo acento en la palabra. El acento en las palabras que contienen un prefijo es predecible, pues sigue las reglas métricas ya presentadas (véase § 1.2.3.1.2). Así, en (16a), la primera sílaba siempre lleva el acento de la palabra, ya sea que esté o no esté prefijada. Por ello, el acento de la palabra 'cho.ki „lavar‟ se mantiene en la primera sílaba, aun cuando esta es prefijada 'me.cho.ki „lavar en la mano‟. Sin embargo, la presencia de una sílaba pesada atrae el acento de la palabra. Así, en (16b), la sílaba pesada “pon”, que además es la forma del prefijo, recibe el acento en 'pon.he.no „caracha en el brazo‟ y, en (16c), la sílaba pesada “roh” lleva el acento en o.'roh.ko „pie huesudo‟. [pp.51-52]
world_status: statement found in an open source

Dicho de otro modo, el acento, generalmente, recae en la primera sílaba, ya sea liviana (2a) o pesada (2b). Sin embargo, cuando la segunda sílaba es pesada, el acento es atraído por esta (2c-2e). (2a) 'a.na „lengua‟ (2b) 'toh.pi „verruga‟ (2c) o.'moh „peca‟ (2d) is.'pan „patilla, sien‟ (2e) ten.'ton „manzana de adán‟
new_statements.translation: At the word level, stress is trochaic but sensitive to syllable weight, as in other Panoan languages (see Valenzuela 2003:107 for Shipibo-Konibo, Zariquiey 2011:124 for Kashibo-Kakataibo). In other words, stress generally falls on the first syllable, whether light (2a) or heavy (2b). However, when the second syllable is heavy, stress is attracted to it (2c-2e). (2a) 'a.na 'tongue', (2b) 'toh.pi 'wart', (2c) o.'moh 'freckle', (2d) is.'pan 'temple', (2e) ten.'ton 'Adam's apple'.
new_statements.citation: Rodríguez Alzza, Ana Carolina. 2015. Prefijos de partes del cuerpo en la lengua iskonawa (Pano, Perú): una descripción sincrónica. Tesis de Maestría en Lingüística, Pontificia Universidad Católica del Perú.
new_statements.locator: §1.2.3.1.2 'Estructura silábica', p.23 (p.29), examples (2a)-(2e); also p.51 on prefixed roots

The same claim is previewed on p.21 (sec. 1.2.3.1 'El sistema prosodico del iskonawa es trocaico pero sensible al peso silabico') and re-applied on pp.51-52 to prefixed roots (…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls within the first two syllables of the word (leftmost foot): on the second syllable if it is closed/heavy ((C)VC, coda n s sh h), otherwise on the first syllable regardless of the first syllable's weight. Equivalent to Zariquiey's (2015:82) formulation quoted by Ingunza 2020: stress on the head of the leftmost foot, trochaic when σ2 is open, iambic when σ2 is closed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described in the accessible sources (Zariquiey 2015 speaks of feet built from the left edge, implying iterative footing, but no secondary-stress statement was seen).
new_statements.exceptions: Some words stress an open second syllable (a.ˈtu 'stomach', hɨ.ˈna 'fire', kɨ.ˈnɨ 'design'); Zariquiey 2015 (via Franco 2022:27 and Ingunza 2020 fn.6) attributes these to a historically closed second syllable whose coda /t/ resurfaces before vowel-initial suffixes (ˈa.tu.t-an 'stomach-ERG'), i.e. diachronically motivated lexical exceptions. Prefixed body-part roots form one prosodic word and follow the same rule ('me.cho.ki, 'pon.he.no, o.'roh.ko; Rodríguez Alzza 2015:51).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level primary stress on (prefixed or bare) roots/citation forms; suffixation can shift stress by restoring latent codas (Franco 2022 ex. 6a-b). Franco 2022:55 adds that stress is realized mainly by pitch and duration and does not affect nasal coarticulation.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Iskonawa (Isconahua, isco1239) spoken by the last elderly speakers on the Callería river (Ucayali, Peru), documented by the PUCP/Tufts Iskonawa documentation project (Zariquiey, Rodríguez Alzza et al., 2010s); no dialect differentiation. Language is obsolescent (a handful of speakers), which Zariquiey 2015 (per Ingunza 2020 fn.6) invokes for irregular iambic forms with light second syllables.

new_statements.quote: si la segunda sílaba de la palabra es abierta, la lengua parece formar pies trocaicos según los cuales la sílaba hacia la izquierda es la que actúa como núcleo de su pie. [...] Sin embargo, si la segunda sílaba de un pie es cerrada, es esta la que se constituye como su núcleo, en lo que representa un caso de sensibilidad al peso silábico en el sistema prosódico del iskonawa [...]. Esto ocurre sin importar si la sílaba a la izquierda es cerrada o abierta [...] [p.83:] el acento primario cae siempre sobre el núcleo del pie métrico más hacia la izquierda, sin importar el tipo de palabra con el que estemos tratando.
new_statements.translation: If the second syllable of the word is open, the language appears to build trochaic feet in which the leftward syllable acts as the head of its foot. [...] However, if the second syllable of a foot is closed, it is that syllable that becomes the head, which is a case of syllable-weight sensitivity in the Iskonawa prosodic system [...]. This happens regardless of whether the syllable to the left is closed or open [...] [p.83:] primary stress always falls on the head of the leftmost metrical foot, whatever type of word we are dealing with.
new_statements.citation: Zariquiey, Roberto. 2015. Bosquejo gramatical de la lengua iskonawa. Lima/Boston: Latinoamericana Editores / CELACP / Revista de Crítica Literaria Latinoamericana. 224 pp.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and type as the catalog record (Rodríguez Alzza 2015: trochaic, weight-sensitive, stress on the first syllable unless the second is heavy), which is in fact modelled on this grammar; Zariquiey 2015 is the primary source and adds that only the closedness of the second (even-position) syllable matters, the first syllable's weight being irrelevant (so is.ˈpan-type and o.ˈmoh-type words are both iambic), that apparent open-syllable iambs mostly have latent final stops (a.ˈtu ~ ˈa.to.t-an), that suffixes such as -n shift stress, and that longer words are not yet analysed beyond 'leftmost foot head'. No contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the head of the leftmost foot, i.e. within the first two syllables: on the first syllable when the second syllable is open (trochee: ˈi.nu, ˈβa.tsi, ˈis.ku, ˈtsan.pu), on the second syllable when the second syllable is closed by /n s ʃ h/ (iamb;ˈkin, tsan.ˈpɨh, a.ˈwin, wa.ˈsin), regardless of whether the first syllable is itself open or closed; the author describes this as weight sensitivity restricted to even-numbered positions. Monosyllables are stressed and lengthened (minimal-word requirement).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described: the author states that nearly all examples are disyllables forming a single foot and that stress in longer words still needs detailed study ('Es necesario todavía conducir estudios más detallados sobre el acento en palabras más largas', p.83); only the claim that primary stress is on the leftmost foot's head is made for longer words.
new_statements.exceptions: A few disyllables carry stress on an open second syllable (a.ˈtu 'estómago', hɨ.ˈna 'candela', hu.ˈpu 'yanchama'); some are plain exceptions, but most have a latent root-final stop that resurfaces before a vowel-initial suffix, after which stress is regular and initial (ˈa.to.t-an 'estómago-ERG', ˈhɨ.na.t-an, ˈhu.pu.t-an) (pp.82-83, ex. 38). Suffixation can move stress: /βai/ [ˈβaj] 'camino' but with instrumental -n [βãˈĩn] (p.71).
new_statements.identity_note: Iskonawa (Isconahua), Panoan, Peru; data from the last five speakers (Juana Campos Meza, Nelita and Isabel Campos Rodríguez, Pablo Rodríguez Sangana, José Rodríguez Pérez) recorded under NSF DEL grant 1160679; no dialect division is made.

sources.note: §4.3 pp.26-27 (after Zariquiey 2015): primary stress assigned by feet built from the left edge; if the second syllable of the foot has no coda the first syllable is stressed ([ˈhũn.tu.ku], [ˈis.ku]), if it has a coda the second is stressed ([pa.ˈβĩŋ.ki], [t͡san.ˈpɨh], [;ˈkin]); some words stress an open second syllable because of a lost coda that resurfaces before vowel-initial suffixes (a.ˈtu ~ ˈa.tu.t-an). §8.3 p.55: stress has no significant effect on nasal coarticulation; author suggests Iskonawa stress is realized by pitch and duration.
